```ts
getErrorRegistry().codes.addList(Object.entries(projectErrors));

export const projectError = (code: ProjectErrorCode, details?: Record<string, unknown>) => err({ code }, { details });
```

Then `projectError("project.name_missing", { field: "name" })` reads like what it is, and `error.code` can be compared with a `ProjectErrorCode`.

When codes are registered in more than one place, check them in a test instead; see [Set up errors in tests](#set-up-errors-in-tests).

## Retry safely

`isRetryable` says a failed call can be repeated without the risk that it runs twice. Retry on it only around the call that failed, not around a larger operation that contains it:

```ts
import { attemptAsync, type Result } from "@codenhub/error";

export async function withRetry<T>(call: () => Promise<T>, attempts = 3): Promise<Result<T>> {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt += 1) {
    const result = await attemptAsync(call);

    if (result.ok || !result.error.isRetryable || attempt === attempts) {
      return result;
    }

    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 250 * 2 ** attempt));
  }
}

const users = await withRetry(() => db.query("select * from users"));
```

Wrap the single database query or the single `fetch`, not a `publish()` function that uploads a file and then saves a record. If the save fails with a retryable `ECONNREFUSED`, repeating `publish()` uploads the file a second time. [The AppError](docs/app-error.md#isretryable) explains why the flag is this strict.

The loop waits 500 ms, then 1 s, between attempts. Add jitter if many clients can fail at the same moment, so they do not all come back at the same moment too.

## Translate messages

Every preset mapping, and any mapping you register with one, carries a `messageKey`. Look the key up in your catalog and fall back to the English message when the catalog has no entry:

```ts
import type { AppError } from "@codenhub/error";

export function errorText(error: AppError, translate: (key: string) => string | undefined): string {
  return (error.messageKey === null ? undefined : translate(error.messageKey)) ?? error.message;
}
```

The keys are stable across releases, and each always carries the same message. [Presets](docs/presets.md) lists every built-in key. To build a catalog in code, read them from the raw mappings:

```ts
import { browserErrorNames, browserErrorPatterns } from "@codenhub/error/registries/browser";

const browserKeys = new Set([...Object.values(browserErrorNames).map((feedback) => feedback.messageKey), ...browserErrorPatterns.map(([, feedback]) => feedback.messageKey)]);
```

ErrorKit does not ship translations. The keys are the contract; the words are yours.

## Report to an error tracker

Report what nobody described yet, plus the failures you have described that are still bugs:

```ts
import type { AppError } from "@codenhub/error";

// Failures only a developer can fix. The presets give them all one shared message.
const BUG_CODES = new Set(["42P01", "42703", "unexpected_failure", "InvalidStateError", "500"]);

export function shouldReport(error: AppError): boolean {
  return error.type === "unknown" || (error.code !== null && BUG_CODES.has(error.code));
}

if (shouldReport(error)) {
  errorTracker.captureException(error.originalError, { tags: { source: error.source ?? "none" } });
}
```

Report `originalError`, not the `AppError`: the original carries the real message and stack. Most trackers also follow an error's `cause`, and an `AppError`'s `cause` is the same original value, so reporting the `AppError` itself works too.

Do not report on `type === "heuristic"` alone. A heuristic match is usually a network failure on the reader's side, and no deploy of yours is going to fix their train going into a tunnel.

## Ignore cancelled requests

Cancelling a request with an `AbortController` makes it fail with an `AbortError`, which the browser preset turns into "The request was cancelled before it finished." When your own code cancelled it, as an effect cleanup or a newer search replacing an older one does, nobody should see that:

```ts
const result = await attemptAsync(() => fetch(url, { signal }));

if (!result.ok && signal.aborted) {
  return; // We cancelled it ourselves.
}
```

Checking `signal.aborted` works with or without the browser preset, and it does not hide an abort that came from somewhere else.

## Set up errors in tests

The global registry is shared by every test in the same file. Replace it in a setup hook so each test starts from the same mappings:

```ts
import { createErrorRegistry, setErrorRegistry } from "@codenhub/error";
import { supabaseErrorRegistry } from "@codenhub/error/registries/supabase";
import { beforeEach } from "vitest";

beforeEach(() => {
  setErrorRegistry(createErrorRegistry([supabaseErrorRegistry]));
});
```

Assert on `code`, `messageKey`, or `type` rather than on `message`. Messages are written for people and get reworded; codes and keys are the stable part. A test that breaks because someone fixed a comma is a test people learn to ignore.

To catch a code your application raises but never registered, list them and check each one against the registry your application builds at startup:

```ts
import { getErrorRegistry } from "@codenhub/error";
import { expect, it } from "vitest";

import { RAISED_CODES } from "../src/errors";
import { setUpErrors } from "../src/setup-errors";

it.each(RAISED_CODES)("registers %s", (code) => {
  setUpErrors();
  expect(getErrorRegistry().codes.get(code)).toBeDefined();
});
```

## Next

The recipes cover the common paths. [Caveats and limitations](docs/caveats.md) covers the uncommon ones: each surprise the package can cause, why it works that way, and what to do instead. Read it once now, and it will save you a debugging session later.

<!-- Source: docs/caveats.md -->

# Caveats and limitations

Everything on this page is deliberate, and every item on it has surprised someone at least once. Each one says what happens, why, and what to do instead. Skim the headings now; when something looks wrong later, the answer is probably here.

## Unmatched text never becomes the message

**What happens:** `createAppError(new Error("Email is required"))` has the message `"An unexpected error occurred."`, not `"Email is required"`. So does `err("Email is required")`.

**Why:** raw error messages are written for developers and often contain table names, file paths, query fragments, or other people's data. ErrorKit only shows text that someone registered on purpose.

**Instead:** raise your own failures with a registered code, `err({ code: "signup.email_missing" })`, or pass a `fallbackMessage` that fits the place you are in.

## A code nobody registered is lost

**What happens:** `createAppError({ code: "project.name_missing" })` is an `"unknown"` error with `code: null` until that code is registered. A typo in the code, or a mapping added in a file that never ran, fails silently.

**Why:** `code` names the mapping that classified the error, so a branch on it only ever sees codes someone described. Keeping the raw code would also send whatever code a database or service produced to the client in `toJSON()`.

**Instead:** raise your own errors through one object of codes, so a typo is a type error, or check the codes in a test; see [Recipes](docs/recipes.md#raise-your-own-errors).

## The global registry is shared state

**What happens:** `getErrorRegistry()` returns one registry per copy of the package, shared by everything that imports that copy. On a server, every request sees the same mappings.

**Why:** it lets you configure errors once, at startup, and normalize anywhere without passing a registry around.

**Instead:** configure the global registry once, before handling any request, and never change it per request; two concurrent requests would see each other's changes. For mappings that only apply in one place, pass `{ registry }` to that call. In tests, reset it with `setErrorRegistry` (see [Recipes](docs/recipes.md#set-up-errors-in-tests)).

## Two copies of the package do not know each other

**What happens:** if your application ends up with two copies of `@codenhub/error`, such as two versions installed side by side, each copy has its own global registry, and `isAppError` from one copy returns `false` for an error made by the other.

**Why:** `isAppError` recognizes only errors this copy created, so that objects shaped like an `AppError`, including ones built from untrusted JSON, are never mistaken for one.

**Instead:** keep one version installed. `pnpm why @codenhub/error` shows where a second copy comes from. An `AppError` from another copy is still normalized, as an ordinary object.

## The last mapping added wins

**What happens:** registering an identifier that already exists replaces it, and `merge` overwrites matching entries. Merging the Supabase preset after your own `23505` mapping replaces yours with the preset's.

**Instead:** merge presets first and add your own mappings last. When two sources use the same codes for different things, give each its own registry; see [Registries](docs/registries.md#the-global-registry-or-your-own).

## Names match any error with that name

**What happens:** with the browser or Node.js preset merged, any error whose `name` is `TimeoutError` is classified as that preset's, including errors from a library that happens to use the same class name. The browser preset does the same for `NotFoundError` and its other names.

**Instead:** classify that library's errors against a registry without the preset, or register a more specific code for them.

## Cancelled requests are errors too

**What happens:** cancelling a `fetch` with an `AbortController` rejects it with an `AbortError`, which the browser preset turns into "The request was cancelled before it finished." That includes cancellations your own code made on purpose.

**Instead:** check whether you cancelled it, and skip showing anything; see [Recipes](docs/recipes.md#ignore-cancelled-requests).

## HTTP status codes are not errors to `fetch`

**What happens:** a `fetch` that receives a `404` or `500` resolves normally. Passing the `Response` to `createAppError` produces an `"unknown"` error, because a response has no code, name, or message to match.

**Instead:** check `response.ok` and classify the status yourself; see [Recipes](docs/recipes.md#classify-http-responses).

## Matching is case-sensitive, except in patterns

**What happens:** a registered message `"Upload failed"` does not match `"upload failed"`. Codes, names, messages, and prefixes are all compared case-sensitively.

**Instead:** register the exact text the failing code produces, or use a pattern with the `i` flag. Trailing punctuation and spaces never matter for messages and prefixes.

## Wrapped errors are searched to a limited depth

**What happens:** `createAppError` looks three levels deep into wrapper fields, and eight levels down a `cause` chain. It reads only the first ten entries of an `errors` list. A failure buried deeper resolves as if it were not there.

**Why:** every level can multiply the number of values to inspect, and the input can come from anywhere. The limits keep the work small on any input.

**Instead:** normalize closer to where the failure happens, or wrap failures with `cause`, which is followed furthest.

## Retryable is narrower than "might work next time"

**What happens:** a response timeout, a reset connection, or a failed `fetch` in the browser is never marked retryable, even though trying again often works.

**Why:** each of those can happen after the server already acted on the request, and repeating a request that already ran can charge a card twice. `isRetryable` promises safety, not likelihood.

**Instead:** retry those yourself only where repeating the request is harmless, such as a `GET`. See [The AppError](docs/app-error.md#isretryable).

## Presets do not cover everything

- The browser preset recognizes a failed `fetch` and a failed `import()` by the messages Chromium, Firefox, and Safari produce today. A browser that rewords them falls back to `"unknown"` until the preset catches up.
- The Node.js preset covers network failures and the errors an `AbortSignal` raises, and was observed on Node.js 24. Other server runtimes may report the same failures differently.
- The Supabase preset covers the Auth codes a person can act on, six PostgreSQL codes, and the client's own error names. It maps the few developer faults a running application commonly hits, such as a missing table or column, to one shared message, so they are `"known"`: report them by `code`, not by type (see [Recipes](docs/recipes.md#report-to-an-error-tracker)). Other codes only a developer can fix, such as `bad_jwt`, are left unmapped on purpose and reach your error tracker as `"unknown"`.

Register your own mapping for anything a preset misses. [Presets](docs/presets.md) lists exactly what each one covers.

## No translations ship with the package

Every preset mapping has a stable `messageKey`, but ErrorKit includes only the English messages. Translate the keys in your own catalog; see [Recipes](docs/recipes.md#translate-messages).

## Structured clone drops the fields

**What happens:** sending an `AppError` through `postMessage`, `structuredClone`, or IndexedDB gives the other side a plain `Error` without `type`, `code`, or the other fields, and on some engines with the raw `cause` attached.

**Instead:** send `error.toJSON()` and rebuild it with `appErrorFromJSON` on the other side; see [The AppError](docs/app-error.md#sending-an-error-across-a-boundary).

## Patterns you write can be slow

A pattern runs against every message `createAppError` sees, and a message can be crafted by someone trying to slow your server down. A pattern with nested repetition, such as `/(a+)+$/`, can take seconds on the wrong input. Keep custom patterns anchored and simple; see [Registries](docs/registries.md#writing-patterns). The built-in patterns are all anchored, with no nested repetition.

## Next

That is the whole package. From here:

- The [API reference](docs/reference/index.md) has every export with its exact signature, for when you need to look something up.
- [Recipes](docs/recipes.md) has the complete solutions, for when you need to build something.
- The [overview](docs/index.md) has the reading path, for when you send this to a colleague.

<!-- Source: docs/changelog/0.3.0.md -->

# 0.3.0

## Added

- `attempt` and `attemptAsync` convert throwing code into a `Result` without a hand-rolled `try`/`catch`, which was the only remaining way to reach `err()` from a throwing boundary. Both validate their options before running the callback.
- `orElse` and `orElseAsync` recover from a failed `Result`, and `all` combines a list of results into one, throwing `TypeError` for an entry that is not a `Result`. Falling back on a specific failure, or collecting the results of parallel calls, took a hand-written `match` or `if` at every call site.
- An HTTP preset at `@codenhub/error/registries/http` maps twelve client and server error statuses, none retryable, for classifying a failed response by its status. Every application that used `fetch` copied the status registry from the recipe.
- Error-boundary adapters: `AppErrorBoundary` at `@codenhub/error/react` and `createAppErrorBoundary` at `@codenhub/error/svelte` hand a React or Svelte fallback a normalized `AppError` and report each caught error once. React 18 or newer and Svelte 5.3 or newer are optional peer dependencies; the core entrypoints still have no dependencies. A fallback written by hand showed the raw thrown message unless every application remembered to normalize it.
- `AppError.details` carries structured data the code attached with the new `details` option, such as the form field that failed, and `toJSON()` and `appErrorFromJSON` carry it across a boundary. It accepts JSON values only, dropping a key whose value is `undefined` as `JSON.stringify` does, and is never read from the raw error. Data like that had nowhere to go but `originalError`, which never leaves the process.
- A generated API reference ships with the package, covering every `exports` subpath.
- A Node.js preset at `@codenhub/error/registries/node` classifies network failures from sockets, DNS, and the built-in `fetch`, such as `ECONNREFUSED`, `ENOTFOUND`, and `UND_ERR_CONNECT_TIMEOUT`. A failed `fetch` on Node.js used to resolve to an unknown error under every built-in preset.
- `AppError.code` holds the registered code that classified the error, or the registered name when no code matched, and `toJSON()` includes it. Consumers can branch on a specific failure without comparing message text or a translation key.
- Entries of an `errors` list, as on `AggregateError`, are classified. The first ten are inspected.
- The Supabase preset maps the Auth codes a person using the application can run into and act on, 41 where it had 10: password rules, existing email and phone, ended sessions, expired links and invitations, two-step verification, suspended accounts, interrupted sign-in flows, and the request rate limit.
- The browser preset classifies a code-split chunk that fails to load, by webpack's `ChunkLoadError` name and by the message Chromium, Firefox, and Safari each produce for a failed `import()`, and tells the reader to reload the page. It also maps the `NotReadableError` and `EncodingError` names.
- The Node.js preset maps `EAI_AGAIN`, `EHOSTUNREACH`, `ENETUNREACH`, and `EPIPE`, and the `TimeoutError` and `AbortError` names an `AbortSignal` raises, exported as `nodeErrorNames`. A `fetch` given `AbortSignal.timeout()` on a server resolved to an unknown error, and merging the browser preset for it told the reader to check their internet connection.
- The Supabase preset classifies two errors the Supabase Auth client raises itself: `AuthSessionMissingError`, which carries no code and is what most calls return without a session, as an ended session, and `pkce_code_verifier_not_found`, from a sign-in link opened in another browser, as an interrupted sign-in. Both resolved to an unknown error.
- `appErrorFromJSON` rebuilds an `AppError` from the shape `toJSON()` produces, so a failure a server sent as JSON can be held in a `Result` on the client. Passing the parsed object to `createAppError` lost every name, message, prefix, and pattern match. The sender chooses the message, so it is for sources the application trusts.
- The `./package.json` subpath is exported, so tools that read the package's metadata can resolve it.
- A `default` export condition, so CommonJS can `require()` the package on runtimes that support requiring ES modules.

## Changed

- **Breaking.** The package requires Node.js 24 or newer, where it declared 22. CI had only ever run it on 24, so the 22 claim was untested; it now names the line CI runs. Browser, worker and edge runtimes are unaffected. ([#203](https://github.com/codenhub/codenhub/issues/203))
- **Breaking.** Strings are classified against the registry at every wrapper depth. Previously only a top-level string bypassed matching, so `err("Failed to fetch")` resolved to the generic fallback while `err({ cause: "Failed to fetch" })` resolved through the registry. A message, prefix, or pattern mapping that matches a top-level string passed to `createAppError` or `err()` now produces a known or heuristic result instead of `unknown`. Registry messages are curated and an unmatched string still resolves to the fallback, so nothing raw reaches a consumer either way.
- **Breaking.** `ok` and `err` results are frozen, so code that mutated one now fails.
- **Breaking.** The browser fetch and network pattern uses its own `error.browser.requestFailed` key rather than `error.browser.network`, so no translation key has to cover two different fallback messages. A translation map covering the old key needs the new one.
- **Breaking.** The browser failed-fetch pattern matches only the whole message an engine produces. Text that merely contains `load failed` or `networkerror`, such as `Config load failed`, is no longer classified as a network failure.
- **Breaking.** `attempt` rejects a callback that returns a promise at the type level, and throws `TypeError` when a callback the type checker cannot see through, such as one typed `any`, returns a promise or other thenable. Its rejection used to escape inside an `Ok`; use `attemptAsync`.
- **Breaking.** The browser `TimeoutError` mapping is not retryable. `isRetryable` means the operation can be repeated without the risk that it runs twice, and a timeout can fire after the server received the request; the Node.js preset already treated response timeouts that way.
- A `cause` chain is followed to a depth of 8 at the default `maxDepth`, where every wrapper field stopped at 3. A failure wrapped once per layer, such as `service → repository → SDK → fetch failed → ECONNREFUSED`, resolved to the generic fetch pattern or to an unknown error; the other fields still stop at 3, where they would multiply the candidates.
- A `messageKey` or `source` is any non-empty string. The repository's naming conventions were enforced at runtime, so an application could not register the keys its translation catalog already had.
- **Breaking.** An existing `AppError` is classified again only when a `registry` is supplied, and then only ever upgraded: a pattern match replaces an unknown error, a known match replaces anything it differs from, and everything else returns the same object. A lone `fallbackMessage`, or the default `maxDepth` written out, used to turn a known error into an unknown one, and a `fallbackMessage` replaced the message of an unknown error, so the message alternated as an error passed through layers that each supplied one. A `fallbackMessage` now words an unknown error only while it still carries the default message, so the first layer to supply one keeps its wording, and a layer that wraps a call whose own layer named no fallback, such as an `unwrap` inside `attemptAsync`, still gets its own. Either option also classified the error against the global registry, replacing a classification made by a per-service registry.
- **Breaking.** The Supabase `FunctionsRelayError` mapping is not retryable, and its message tells the reader to check whether the call went through. The relay reports the error on a response, after the function may have run.
- **Breaking.** An `AppError` is no longer frozen. Its own properties still cannot be changed or removed, but new ones can be added: Koa's error handler assigns `status` and hapi's `Boom.boomify` assigns `isBoom` to every error they catch, and on a frozen `AppError` that assignment threw. In Koa the rejection went unhandled, which ends a Node.js process. `Object.isFrozen(error)` is now `false`. The `stack` stays unlocked, because a library that rethrows a caught error calls `Error.captureStackTrace` on it, and on a locked stack that call throws.
- **Breaking.** An `AppError` nested in another value keeps its classification unless a `registry` is supplied. Wrapping one, as in `new Error("checkout failed", { cause: appError })`, used to have the raw value inside it classified against the global registry, which replaced an unknown or heuristic classification made by a per-service registry and could mark the result retryable. A supplied `registry` now also rewords a nested known `AppError`, as it already did one passed directly; the nested one used to end the search.
- `mapAsync` and `andThenAsync` accept a mapper that returns a plain value or `Result` as well as a promise, so a mapper that is asynchronous only on some paths type-checks.
- **Breaking.** The Supabase rate-limit mappings are not retryable. `isRetryable` carries no delay, so code that retried on it did so at once and counted against the limit again; the message tells the reader how long to wait.
- **Breaking.** Every preset message is rewritten to say what happened and what to do next, where it used to restate the code: `invalid_credentials` reads "We couldn't sign you in. The email or password is incorrect. Check them and try again." Failures only a developer can fix, such as a missing table or column, share one message that tells the reader the problem is not their doing and names no internals. The `messageKey` values are unchanged.
- **Breaking.** The `"unexpected"` `AppErrorType` is renamed `"heuristic"`. The type says how an error was matched, not how serious it is, and the old name invited `type === "unexpected"` as a test for a defect, which reports an offline user matched by a pattern and misses a missing table matched by its code.
- **Breaking.** `appErrorFromJSON` rebuilds every error with `isRetryable: false`. The sender's flag describes a call the sender made, such as its own database call, so a client that retried the request on it could repeat a request the sender had already acted on. It also normalizes as raw input a value whose fields `toJSON()` cannot produce together, such as an unknown error with a `code` or an empty `messageKey`.
- **Breaking.** The `codes`, `names`, and `messages` buckets' `values()` return a frozen list of `[identifier, feedback]` entries, as the prefix and pattern buckets already returned a list. The iterator they returned had no `length`, and calling `.map` on it worked only on runtimes with iterator helpers.

## Fixed

- The browser failed-fetch pattern and `TimeoutError`, the Node.js `fetch failed` pattern, and the Supabase `FunctionsFetchError` and `FunctionsHttpError` messages tell the reader to check whether the request went through before trying again. They said to try again, and the failed-fetch messages said the server was never reached, although each can follow a request the server already ran, as a CORS block or a dropped response does. The `messageKey` values are unchanged.
- The Node.js preset messages speak about "a service this depends on" and no longer tell the reader to check their internet connection. The preset runs where the failing call was made, most often a server calling another service, so the reader's own connection was not the one that failed. The `messageKey` values are unchanged.
- Normalizing a message is linear in its length. A long message with a run of `.`, `!` or `?` inside it took quadratic time, with or without registered mappings: 80 KB took over seven seconds.
- `attempt` and `attemptAsync` reject an out-of-range `maxDepth` before running the callback. It used to surface only when the callback failed, replacing the real failure.
- A `DOMException` is classified by its name; its legacy numeric `code` could match an unrelated registered code.
- A message or prefix mapping whose trailing punctuation is broken up by whitespace, such as `Done . .`, matches. Its key was normalized once when stored and again on lookup, to a different result, so it never matched until the registry was merged or frozen.
- `attempt` and `attemptAsync` throw `TypeError` for a callback that is not a function instead of returning an `Err`.
- An `AppError` no longer exposes the class that builds it: `constructor` is `Error` and the shared prototype is frozen, so an `AppError` cannot be built around `createAppError` and `appErrorFromJSON`, and `toJSON` cannot be replaced for every instance.
- Feedback without a message returned by a hand-written registry throws `TypeError` instead of producing an `AppError` with no message.

## Removed

- **Breaking.** The browser `connection refused|dns_probe_finished` pattern and its `error.browser.connectionRefused` key. No browser is known to produce that text in an error message, and it classified unrelated server messages relayed to the client as a retryable browser network failure.
- **Breaking.** The Supabase `invalid_grant` mapping and its `error.supabase.auth.invalidGrant` key. It is not among the codes Supabase Auth publishes, so it could not match.
- The internal `createUntrustedAppError` variant, made redundant by classifying strings at every depth.
